sources.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
sources.text: Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. stories.title: AI costs: what teams pay to use AI tools
stories.summary: AI costs explained: how AI tools are priced, what drives a team's bill, and how to compare plans by cost per task.

sources.name: Perplexity
sources.title: AI costs: what teams pay to use AI tools
sources.text: How AI tools are priced, what drives a team's bill, and how to compare plans by the work they get done. AI costs are what a team pays to use AI tools. They fall into three types: Take a hypothetical 10-person team paying $25 per person per month for an AI research tool. The subscription is a fixed $250. In busy months, two analysts run out of included credits and the team buys $100 more, so the bill runs to $350. Rollout adds 18 hours of staff time that never appears on an invoice: eight hours for an operations lead to connect the tool to the company's sign-in system, and an hour of training for each of the 10 team members. AI tools use seven main pricing models. Many plans combine two or more, such as a subscription with included credits. Grammarly's free plan includes a monthly allowance of AI prompts Testing whether a tool fits a team's work before paying for it GitHub Copilot Business is billed per user each month Teams where most people use the tool regularly and at similar levels Claude's Max plan offers 5 or 20 times the usage of its Pro plan People who regularly hit standard limits or run multi-step tasks Adobe's Creative Cloud plans include a monthly allocation of generative credits Teams whose heavy AI work comes in bursts, such as campaign launches Perplexity's Sonar API (for adding search-based answers to other apps) charges by length of questions and answers plus a flat fee per question Teams with technical staff building AI into their own products or workflows Microsoft 365 Copilot is an annual per-user enterprise add-on to Microsoft 365 Organizations that need security reviews and central administration Intercom's Fin charges per outcome, such as a resolved customer conversation High-volume work with a countable result, such as customer support Free plans charge nothing but cap how much each person can use the tool, and they usually leave out the most capable models and some features. When a person reaches the cap, the tool stops handling that type of request or switches to a less capable model until the limit resets. A seat is a license for one named user, and per-seat plans charge a set price for each seat, billed monthly or annually. Team versions usually add admin controls, such as deciding who has access. The bill scales with headcount rather than with use, so a person who runs two queries a week costs the same as one who runs 200. Premium tiers are higher-priced individual plans with higher usage limits, more capable models, or more advanced features. They're still priced per person, so a team pays the higher rate only for each person it upgrades. Credit plans include a monthly allowance that tasks use up at different rates. Usually complex tasks use more credits than simple ones. When the allowance runs out, people can wait for it to reset or buy more. Unused credits often expire. Credits usually sit on top of a subscription rather than replacing it. Teams that build AI into their own software or workflows pay through an API, which lets software send requests to an AI model directly. API usage is billed per token (small chunk of text). A short, common word is usually one token, while longer words are split into two or more. Both the text sent to the model and the text it generates count toward the bill. Some APIs add per-request fees on top. Enterprise plans combine seats with advanced security and administration features, such as single sign-on and controls over how long data is stored. Pricing is typically annual, and listed per seat or set by quote. Some enterprise AI plans are add-ons that require a separate base license, so their cost comes on top of software the company already pays for. Outcome-based pricing charges for a completed result rather than for access or usage, so the bill depends on how the vendor defines a result. Intercomâs Fin, for example, bills only once per customer conversation. Standard individual plans for the most widely used AI tools cost about $20 a month. Premium individual tiers run $100 to $500. Business seats cost about $14 to $40 per user per month. Business: $20 billed annually, $25 monthly $20 billed annually, plus usage at API rates Google Workspace Business Standard: $14 billed annually, $16.80 monthly Google Workspace Enterprise: custom quote Copilot Business: $18-$21 billed annually, plus a Microsoft 365 plan Microsoft 365 Copilot: $30 billed annually, plus a Microsoft 365 plan Prices in USD as of October 2026. Prices are subject to change. Check vendor websites for current pricing. Development teams may spend more on AI than other teams, because coding tools increasingly run agents. To take one example, Anthropic reports that Claude Code averages about $13 per developer per active day, or $150 to $250 per developer per month, across enterprise deployments. For comparison, a standard seat on Anthropic's business plan costs $20 per user per month, or roughly $1 per active day for someone who stays within the plan's included usage. Using Gemini pricing as an example, Gartner suggests budgeting by usage level : Agent workflows or high-volume automated tasks Take a hypothetical 10-person development team on a plan that charges $20 per seat plus usage. 6 developers using the tool on most working days 1 developer running coding agents most of the day This is a modest budget for a team using AI tools with restraint. If a developer uses frontier models 24/7 across multiple agents, costs can compound quickly. And as a developer team uses AI tools more aggressively, expect the costs to increase. Four factors shape what a team spends on AI tools: On seat-based plans, the bill depends on how many people need their own login, not on how many people benefit from the tool's output. A research lead might use an AI tool to produce a report that 10 colleagues read, but only the research lead will need a seat. Team plans often set a minimum number of seats, so a very small team can end up paying for more seats than it uses. Every step an AI t

sources.title: What Are MCP Tools and How Do AI Models Use Them?
sources.text: Learn what MCP tools are, how AI models find and call them through MCP servers, and how to use them safely. MCP tools are functions an AI model can call to perform a task outside the conversation. For example, search your notes or query a database. Each tool sits on an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and has a name and a short description that help the model decide when to use it. The term "MCP tool" is used in other ways too. In everyday use, people say "MCP tools" when they mean MCP servers (the applications that offer tools) or the directories that list those servers. MCP Tools is also the name of a command-line program for listing and calling the tools on an MCP server. This guide is about the protocol functions, not servers, directories, or command lines. It explains what a tool consists of, the kinds of tools servers offer, and how tools differ from resources, prompts, and function calling. It then walks through the steps a model takes to use a tool, and closes with the most common problems related to their use. An MCP tool is a function that lets AI models complete tasks with other software applications. For instance, my AI agents and workflows use MCP tools to draft emails in Gmail ( create_draft ), create Trello cards ( trelloWriteCard ), and pull live search results from DataForSEO ( serp_organic_live_advanced ), to name just a few. Software apps often offer multiple MCP tools on their MCP servers. For example, the Trello MCP server currently has 14 MCP tools that enable AI models to read and update boards, lists, checklists, cards, and more. And because MCP standardizes how tools are described and offered, any AI app that supports the protocol can use the same MCP tool. Some tools add extra metadata: a display name, a description of the results they return (an output schema), and annotations about how the tool behaves. The AI model never sees the code behind a tool. It works from what the tool says about itself, so a vague name or description leads the model to pick the wrong tool. MCP tools fall into four groups by what they do: Besides MCP tools, an MCP server can offer two other types of building blocks, which the protocol calls primitives: resources and prompts. For example, GitHub's official MCP server offers: The difference is what each one does and who decides when to use one: you, the AI app you're working in (e.g., Perplexity), or the AI model running inside that app. An AI model uses an MCP tool in five steps: discovery, tool selection, invocation, results, and error handling. Your AI app passes everything between the model and the server. Say you ask your AI app to check your Trello "This week" list and draft an email to your editor with an update. Here's what happens end to end: The key point is that the model chooses tools from their descriptions alone, and your AI app does all the talking to servers. Problems with MCP tools come down to four things: how many tools are connected, how they're named and described, how much data they return, and which servers they come from. Here's what each problem looks like and what helps: Every tool definition sits in the model's context window before you've asked anything, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Connect only the servers a task needs, and turn off unused tools where your AI app allows it. Example: GitHub's MCP server lets you enable only the groups of tools (toolsets) you need. The model calls the wrong tool, or the right one with the wrong inputs, because two descriptions sound alike or one says too little. Provide clear, specific names and descriptions, ideally with an example of when to use the tool. If a server's tools keep misfiring, MCP Inspector, the official testing tool, shows exactly what each tool says about itself. Two servers each offer a tool called search , and there's no telling which one a call is meant for. Prefix tool names with the server's name. Example: Trello's server ( trelloSearch , trelloReadList ). A tool returns more than the task needs, such as a whole email thread with its formatting, and crowds the model's context. Use tools that offer compact formats. Example: Gmail's get_thread tool description recommends plain-text format "to prevent context exhaustion." A careless or malicious server could use tool calls to pull data out of your conversation. Connect servers only from sources you trust, and keep approvals on for tools that change things or send data out. MCP tools need your approval because, without it, the AI model could make changes you didn't intend or share sensitive data with a server you don't control. A misread request or a vaguely described tool can trigger the wrong action. Every call also sends some of your information to a server. That's why the protocol expects AI apps to keep a person in the loop, with the ability to deny any tool call. Here's a practical way to sort tools by how much checking they need: Perplexity works with MCP tools in both directions: it can use tools from MCP servers you connect, and it offers its own tools to other AI apps. No, MCP isn't just tool calling. Tool calling is how the model asks for a tool, and MCP is how the AI app finds tools and routes each call to the server that runs it. Tool calling (also called function calling) is the AI model's part of the job: the model sees a list of tools and replies with a request to run one. With tool calling alone, each AI app has to define and run every tool itself. MCP lets tools live on servers, so any AI app that supports MCP can offer them to its model and send the model's requests to the right server. No, MCP won't replace APIs, because MCP and APIs work together. MCP tools often sit on top of existing APIs, and when the model calls a tool, the MCP server typically makes an API request. sources.title: Harmonic Security raises $50M to govern how employees use AI tools
sources.text: Workplace artificial intelligence security startup Harmonic Security Inc. today announced it has raised $50 million in new funding to grow its platform for governing how employees use AI tools. The company’s platform inspects anything an employee sends to an AI tool at work before it gets there. Custom small language models read each interaction in context, and a verdict comes back within milliseconds. Live credentials pasted into a chat window are one example of what the system is tuned to catch, according to Harmonic. A developer referencing a database schema should pass. Those checks originally ran only in the browser, and over the past year Harmonic has extended them to desktop AI applications and agentic workflows. In Harmonic’s view, those tools are where problems such as employees signing in to AI services with personal accounts tend to start. Co-founder and Chief Executive Alastair Paterson said “every board I talk to” now wants to know whether AI is delivering value, on top of how to reduce the risk of using it. Harmonic’s answer is a Usage Intelligence layer that runs on the same models. Leaders can see which AI use cases are paying off, down to individual employees who have worked out a faster way to get their jobs done. Outside its own platform, Harmonic has been plugging into tools enterprises already use. Agent Builder, which Cisco Systems Inc. announced for its Cloud Control platform at Cisco Live in June , lists Harmonic among its ecosystem integrations. The connection runs over Model Context Protocol. A second integration, with the Claude Compliance API from Anthropic PBC, pulls activity logs from Anthropic-hosted Claude Platform deployments into Harmonic. Organizations on Claude Enterprise also get the content of conversations. More than 100 companies are customers, some of them among the largest enterprises in the world, and Harmonic said millions of their employees are covered. Climb Global Solutions Inc. and Distology Ltd. have signed on as distribution partners. Staff numbers have passed 90 across the U.S. and the U.K., and the new money will pay for more engineering and go-to-market hires on both sides of the Atlantic. That cash comes from an oversubscribed Series B round led by Crosspoint Capital Partners LP, and existing investors also took part. Before this, the company’s most recent raise was the $17.5 million Series A that Next47 led in October 2024 . Security “has too often slowed the adoption of new technology,” according to Zach Sivertson, a managing director at Crosspoint. Organizations taking up AI should not have to give up control to move quickly, he said, adding that Harmonic gives leaders the visibility to roll AI out sooner. Paterson said the company has “real momentum” and that the round lets it build faster as the AI market keeps changing. Investors have now put $76 million into Harmonic. stories.title: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices
stories.summary: Anthropic's latest research adds to the growing safety concerns around AI from the ability for models to carry out cyberattacks to the technology going rogue.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices
sources.text: Anthropic said Monday that small AI models are "months away" from developing the capabilities needed to replicate themselves across internet-connected devices in the home, marking the latest warning from the frontier lab about the technology's potential safety risks. Anthropic described how AI models could potentially infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens or Android TV boxes, and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without relying on expensive data centers. The AI model would be "challenging to shut down," Anthropic said in a blog post, "since there's no centralized point to shut off." The company acknowledged that there is not yet a "fully rogue replicator." Agents are, however, "becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said. Anthropic's latest research adds to growing safety concerns around AI, such as the ability for models to carry out cyberattacks and the technology going rogue. In September, improvements in frontier models sparked industry-wide warnings of existential risks to humanity. Executives and researchers at Anthropic and rival OpenAI repeatedly warned about the potential risks of increasingly powerful AI, with some calling for tighter guardrails and measures to control the pace of the technology's development . Anthropic said it carried out various tests to see if AI could self-replicate. One of those tests involved running a small Google model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, across a network of 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes. The company noted that these types of devices often have weak security, which could allow a model to infiltrate them. A model that is too large to fit on one device could "split into pieces, or shards" and run across multiple devices, Anthropic said. "In practice, an AI worm wouldn't necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic 'worst case scenario' attack," Anthropic said. It's still "uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take," the AI lab said, warning that it could be a "slow, distributed" system sitting on insecure devices or a "powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits." "As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," Anthropic said. "The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves," the company added.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
sources.text: “Small weight-based replicators” could usher in a new generation of computer worms. AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output. The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against. This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. “Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said . “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.” Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps. Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs. “These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said. The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.) The company said that 30B-parameter models can already complete many of the individual replication steps now, although they make mistakes when performing end-to-end replication. The company went on to say that if small models continue to improve at their current pace, they may be able to achieve the same limited results by the end of the year and that “small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.” The experiment leaves various important considerations unanswered. For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed. This tool is used during development and debugging but should never be used in production settings, because it gives attackers access to the entire device stack. And for another, the replication wasn’t performed by the small models themselves, but rather with GLM-5.2 to orchestrate the process while the targets ran a smaller Llama model. Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own. “Despite the well-designed experimen

sources.title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
sources.text: Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: Gemini 4 Argon finalmente chega ao app e à busca do Google; saiba mais
sources.text: O Google começou a liberar o Gemini 4 Argon para mais usuários nesta terça-feira (13). O modelo de inteligência artificial (IA), anunciado no fim de setembro, está disponível para assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e AI Ultra no aplicativo Gemini e no Modo IA da busca do Google. A novidade também chega à plataforma de desenvolvimento Antigravity, mas, nesse caso, o acesso exige uma assinatura Ultra. Segundo o Google, o Argon foi desenvolvido para lidar com tarefas complexas de raciocínio e melhorar o desempenho em diferentes tipos de trabalho. A empresa também afirma que o modelo responde de maneira mais direta, reduz repetições e clichês e segue instruções de estilo com mais consistência. Ainda não há confirmação sobre a disponibilidade para usuários gratuitos ou assinantes de outros planos. No aplicativo Gemini , o modelo passa a integrar as opções disponíveis para assinantes dos planos Pro e Ultra. Antes, o acesso inicial estava restrito ao plano Ultra. A lista de modelos disponíveis para esses usuários inclui o 3.5 Flash-Lite, o 3.8 Flash, o 3.1 Pro e o 4 Argon. O Google também está modificando a interface do aplicativo para facilitar a alternância entre conversas e tarefas. A opção de tarefas, anteriormente chamada Spark, terá um botão próprio na janela principal do chat. Outra novidade envolve a versão do Gemini para macOS. O aplicativo passará a oferecer acesso direto à interface de programação com agentes do Antigravity , permitindo alternar entre conversas e atividades de codificação para desenvolver aplicativos, experiências na web e outros projetos. De acordo com a empresa, o modelo também consegue compartilhar atualizações sobre o andamento de tarefas mais longas com maior frequência. A proposta é manter os usuários informados enquanto o sistema trabalha em solicitações que exigem mais tempo. O Google afirma que já utiliza o Argon em projetos internos. Um dos exemplos envolve o navegador Chrome: o modelo ajudou a separar o processamento central de páginas da web de uma pasta legada com cerca de 6 milhões de linhas de código, dentro de uma base de código do Chromium que soma 40 milhões de linhas. Segundo a empresa, o trabalho envolveu alterações em centenas de arquivos e permitiu concluir em semanas uma refatoração arquitetural que levaria meses. O objetivo é viabilizar a movimentação de páginas abertas entre abas, painéis laterais e janelas flutuantes sem recarregamento, além de eliminar uma categoria de falhas do navegador. Outro caso citado envolve o Gemma 4 E2B. Com o uso do vLLM em uma GPU A100, o Google relata ter alcançado uma aceleração de 2,85 vezes na inferência de ponta a ponta , elevando a taxa de processamento de aproximadamente 37.900 para mais de 108 mil tokens por segundo. A empresa afirma que o resultado foi obtido em poucos dias, sem perda de qualidade e com 100% de equivalência entre os tokens. No YouTube, o Argon ajudou a reduzir pela metade o uso de CPU da interface de comentários. A análise identificou que a renderização redundante de emojis representava quase 45% da sobrecarga do servidor. Após 12 otimizações, a latência de carregamento dos comentários no servidor caiu 30 milissegundos, enquanto a latência de ponta a ponta no cliente diminuiu 20 milissegundos. Além do aplicativo Gemini e do Modo IA da busca do Google, o modelo está disponível pela Gemini API , com preço promocional de US$ 2 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 10 por milhão de tokens de saída até 30 de novembro de 2026. Após o fim do período promocional, os valores passarão para US$ 4 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 20 por milhão de tokens de saída. O acesso ao modelo no Antigravity para desktop, na interface de linha de comando (CLI) do Antigravity, no AI Studio e no Android Studio Canary exige o plano Google AI Ultra. O Google também abriu inscrições para um programa voltado à comunidade científica. A iniciativa prevê oferecer gratuitamente, durante seis meses, o nível mais alto de uso do Antigravity a 10 mil cientistas . A empresa ainda afirma que o Argon apresenta resultados competitivos em áreas como programação, segurança cibernética, ciência, finanças e direito. Em avaliações de referência, o Google diz que o modelo supera concorrentes como GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1 e Claude Opus 5.5 em diferentes categorias. Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

sources.title: IA mais poderosa do Google, Gemini 4 Argon chega para assinantes Pro e Ultra na web
sources.text: O Google liberou, nesta terça-feira (13), o Gemini 4 Argon para assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e AI Ultra . Descrito pela empresa como seu modelo de inteligência artificial mais poderoso até o momento, ele está disponível no aplicativo Gemini e na versão web, com melhorias em raciocínio, programação e execução autônoma de tarefas. Antes restrito a um grupo menor de usuários, o modelo passou por ajustes de segurança contra jailbreaks , tentativas de contornar as proteções da IA. A versão pública também apresenta respostas mais objetivas, com menos repetições e frases genéricas, além de atualizações frequentes sobre o andamento de tarefas demoradas. Um dos destaques é a integração com mais de 40 aplicativos , como Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe e Shopify. O sistema pode executar atividades, como compras de supermercado, reservas em restaurantes e trabalhos de design, inclusive sem que o usuário precise acompanhar cada etapa diante do computador. O modelo ainda recebeu melhorias na comunicação , com respostas diretas e menos hesitação, além de atualizações sobre o progresso de operações longas. A proposta é tornar as interações mais claras e facilitar o acompanhamento de tarefas complexas. Além de responder a perguntas, o Gemini pode assumir atividades que envolvem diferentes etapas e serviços. Para isso, o usuário pode alternar entre o bate-papo convencional e o modo de tarefas por meio de um botão na janela principal do chat. Nesse segundo modo, a IA executa ações de forma autônoma e se conecta a dezenas de aplicativos, conforme as instruções recebidas e os recursos disponíveis em cada plataforma. Na programação, os avanços incluem melhorias na geração de código e a integração do Google Antigravity ao aplicativo Gemini para macOS. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ Quais são os modelos do Gemini? Conheça as IAs disponíveis no app do Google ”.

sources.title: Singapore office and government MOU
sources.text: Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI. “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.” Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.” “Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.” Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil. Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models. We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index , and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI. In our latest Economic Index , Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict. In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense. In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements. Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code. This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers. Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders. Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our careers page . Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms. We’re publishing a new version of our Usage Policy.
